This study presents a novel adaptive time-series learning framework called TV-PAR to effectively manage changing patterns of data over time and learn dynamic models simultaneously. The proposed TV-PAR model combines a parameter-estimating algorithm and a scheme for updating models based on changing patterns, allowing it to accurately forecast future values of a time-series process that follows a Poisson distribution. To evaluate the TV-PAR model's performance and effectiveness, we developed an optimal offline learning algorithm that aims to learn models in a way that generates the smallest possible error. We also conducted a performance assessment by comparing the TV-PAR model to an existing adaptive model and an offline learning approach in various scenarios with different data patterns.

A system consisting of a telescope and a camera allows for atmospheric aerosol detection by analyzing how light from the sky is scattered. A key benefit of this method is its ability to provide detailed vertical information about aerosols. A single telescope-camera system can determine aerosol thickness at various heights, while a network of these systems can create a three-dimensional map of aerosol density. This technique has been enhanced by recent developments in using a machine learning model to rapidly determine aerosol data and a new approach to calculating aerosol optical depth at different heights. This new standard of performance has enabled this method to be ranked as one of the most accurate techniques for assessing aerosol thickness by the International Aerosol Standardization Organization.

Numerous configurational sampling methods have been developed for molecular dynamics simulations, with some even employing Langevin dynamics. This study investigates the connection between the fluctuations observed in Langevin dynamics simulations and configurational sampling algorithms like Metropolis or ace algorithms. It is found that the time-dependent harmonic oscillator solution provides an exact framework for calculating these fluctuations, allowing for efficient and practical configurational sampling. A new algorithm, called RWA-NVE, is introduced that utilizes the oscillatory fluctuations of particles in harmonic potentials, resulting in significant improvements in both acceptance rates and sampled configurations compared to traditional methods. Notably, simulations using the RWA-NVE algorithm with anharmonic potentials that mimic molecular configurations yield nearly identical configurations as those simulated using anharmonic potentials directly. This research demonstrates that the particle's fluctuation time correlation mirrors the molecular configuration distribution, enabling rapid and efficient configurational sampling even in complex scenarios.

Human-generated descriptions serve as the gold standard for evaluating image description systems, which rely on text data for learning and generating descriptions. However, creating high-quality descriptions to match every image is impractical and expensive. To address this challenge, our research aims to develop a new evaluation method that utilizes existing human-generated descriptions, either directly or in a compared format, to assess image description accuracy. We propose three novel metrics: compared ranking, compared embedding, and compared similarity, which leverage the human descriptions to create a more precise ranking of image descriptions. Our approach yields significantly better results compared to existing methods, resulting in a 25.6% improvement in accuracy when using compared ranking and a 23.1% improvement when using compared similarity.

A specific subset of conformal field theories, particularly those in two dimensions, can be analytically characterized through a set of closed equations known as Euler-Arnold equations. This distinct category of theories includes well-known examples such as the W$_3$ minimal models and the $BCD$ conformal coset theories. Notably, Fuchs, Frho, and Zwanziger derived these equations in 1993; however, their work appears to be largely unknown. This unacknowledged contribution builds upon earlier findings by Balachandran, Marmigg, and Skyrme from 1980 and 1981.

Predictions based on a new kind of symmetry called an extended Baryon number symmetry are presented. This Baryon number symmetry could potentially explain the existence of extra Baryons and Mesons beyond the standard model, and may also explain dark matter. If such a scenario occurs, Baryons and Mesons composed of three or more types of particles would be forecasted as the most basic form, with Baryons consisting of two new kinds of particles (Q1, Q2) and one standard particle (q) being the most likely type. In this scenario, quarks of the new kind would likely behave similarly to regular quarks in terms of their behavior when broken down. Forecasts for specific extra Baryons and Mesons are provided, including those made of three new kinds of particles or two new kinds of particles and one standard particle, with certain assumptions about the new kind of quarks' properties. Assuming the new quarks behave similarly to regular quarks, extra Baryons composed of three new kinds of particles would likely decay quickly, but those composed of two new kinds of particles and one standard particle could potentially be stable. If a new kind of quark with a similar mass to the top quark exists, it would likely behave similarly to the top quark in terms of its behavior when broken down. A new approach has been taken to establish the optimal wideband waveforming schemes for IDPT that utilize a single antenna and a single carrier, both in SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM scenarios. Building upon previous results that established the schemes using multiple antennas and multiple carriers, significant additional gains have been found, particularly in the SISO-OFDM scenario with a power convex constraint. It was discovered that using two transmitters with a PCC outperforms using a single transmitter with three antennas and three carriers, resulting in a 33.5% gain in average throughput. Similarly, using two transmitters with three levels of PSK achieves a 26.7% better average throughput than using a single transmitter with three antennas, three carriers, and a PCC.

Developing and updating probability density functions (PDFs) necessitates a precise theoretical framework that accounts for both data inconsistencies and underlying physical principles. This document outlines a comprehensive theoretical framework used in PDF fitting experiments, addressing key physical processes, measurement types, and specific analysis scenarios. It is crucial to note that this framework is specifically designed for PDF fitting applications, distinct from other uses in theoretical physics.

Initially, an oscillatory reaction occurs when the jet is forced at a frequency of 10 Hz. However, when the forcing frequency shifts to 20 Hz, a steady flame emerges. When the forcing frequency returns to 10 Hz, a sudden flame instability occurs. When a steady flame is established, further frequency increases lead to a decline in oscillatory amplitudes. When an oscillatory reaction is present, a frequency increase results in a decrease in amplitudes. When the forcing frequency at an oscillatory reaction exceeds the flame's fundamental frequency, a shift to its harmonic occurs. When the forcing frequency exceeds 20 Hz, no reaction occurs even when entering the jet's shear layer. When the forcing frequency at a steady flame exceeds 20 Hz, a weak oscillatory reaction emerges. When the acoustic forcing frequency matches the flame's fundamental frequency at an oscillatory reaction, a shift to its harmonic occurs. When the frequency returns to the fundamental, a return to the original oscillatory pattern occurs. When the frequency at a steady flame returns to 1 Hz, a weak oscillatory reaction appears. Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. It is based on a fourth-rank tensor called the curvature tensor, which can be used to define essential tetrads without relying on an auxiliary metric. This paper demonstrates that Nonlocal gravity is equivalent to a specific special case of a general nonlocal gravity theory where the fundamental tensor is constant and affects all events. This results in a model where the gravity field affects gravity itself, leading to a consistent description of physical phenomena.

This paper outlines a comprehensive plan for utilizing the minor systems at the LHC, with a focus on their upgraded versions, to conduct a wide-ranging search for new physics beyond the Standard Model. The plan covers the energy ranges and luminosity targets for each system, as well as the potential discovery reach in mass scales for various types of new phenomena, including extra dimensions, first-order phase transitions, and sector standards models. Additionally, the paper provides an overview of the proposed search strategies and experimental techniques, including the use of magnetic calorimeters, the operation of calorimeters at extremely low temperatures, and the development of sophisticated algorithms for data analysis. The document also highlights the significance of exploring new physics beyond the mass scale range of the LHC and the HLHC, the potential contributions of the minor systems to our understanding of new physics, and the potential applications in new physics research.

Determining the nature of the variable X-ray sources observed within the Milky Way's central basin is a complex task, influenced by both their optical and X-ray properties. A key factor in classifying these sources is identifying whether they contain a compact stellar companion that is either neutron star or black, as this information impacts their expected behavior, spectral characteristics, and even their potential binary system configurations. One method used to analyze these sources involves estimating the recurrence period of X-ray flares, which can provide insight into the nature of the compact object by correlating with the periodicity of optical variability, if present. A previous study identified 33 transient X-ray binaries containing a neutron star in the Milky Way, which should also include their recurrence periods, assuming their outburst patterns are similar to M31NE1, a certain near-Earth neutron star X-ray binary with a known recurrence period. After conducting a thorough analysis, a list of 47 candidate neutron star X-ray binary recurrence periods was compiled, ranging from about 50 days to over 1000 days. Notably, this list excludes sources with uncertain or missing period estimates, as well as those with a known black hole component. It is essential to note that determining the recurrence period of these X-ray binaries is not a guaranteed method for distinguishing between neutron star and black hole varieties, although it can provide valuable information on the binary system's characteristics, including the nature of the compact object and the mass distribution of its stellar companion.

A well-known polynomial-time algorithm has been developed by Baker to resolve large random graphs into components. A key step in this algorithm involves dividing a given graph's vertices into two subsets on a cross-product graph. Since these graphs are bipartite, this division can be achieved by identifying a maximum matching within the graph's edge set. A notable theorem by Rota and Taylor ensures that an optimal set of matchings exists, which corresponds to a tiling of the graph's grid representation. In the case of a square grid, this tile pattern forms a checkerboard design. To apply this pattern to a given grid-sized graph, researchers have established a method that involves identifying two disjoint vertex subsets. This process has been found to be fixed-parameter tractable in terms of the graph's size, based on the size of the desired subsets.

The widespread adoption of low-power processors in edge and embedded devices has created a pressing need to optimize performance per watt through instruction set innovation. This paper proposes a revolutionary, energy-efficient processor architecture, HyperDegrade, which reduces the CPU frequency from GHz to MHz ranges. This design change enables significant performance per watt gains, outperforming existing low-power processors by an order of magnitude. HyperDegrade's innovative pipelining strategy, which delays instruction execution until the operating frequency drops, allows for high performance at low frequencies. This allows for a 10 to 100 times performance boost in critical benchmarks, resulting in an impressive 50 to 100 times improvement in performance per watt. HyperDegrade's code size increase, which is a concern for binary translation, is addressed by implementing a compact, 128-bit instruction set. This results in a 2 to 5 times code size growth, which is manageable. HyperDegrade's design is fully functional and verified through a working, cycle-accurate simulator. This simulator demonstrates HyperDegrade's exceptional performance, achieving a 20 to 50 times performance per watt improvement over existing low-power processors.

A localized alteration in knot diagrams enables the distinction between classical and welded knots, allowing various properties to apply uniquely to each type. Crossing alterations such as Reidemeister moves and the unknotting process have this defining characteristic, which the authors term "localization of the property." Unknotting the welded circle, or a welded knot that has no entangled loops, results in an open path. This unconnected set of points is considered a "point-set." Although point-sets are not knot representations, they are still part of the knot theory spectrum. The new unwinding method presented here for both classical and welded knots meets the localized property criterion, differentiating it from other move sets like the braid group motions. This new procedure yields the point-set for the welded circle and the unconnected set of lines for the classical circle. This new method joins previously identified patterns in the knot theory spectrum.

In a partially observable Markov chain domain, a short-horizon look-ahead algorithm that performs control actions in discrete sets has been developed. This algorithm, which combines model-free and partially-specified partial exchange, enables a team of limited robots to achieve a specific objective by implementing a tactical action in a particular area. To accomplish this objective, the robots must eliminate all possible actions that lead to a policy resulting in the desired outcome. This policy, which serves as the optimal course of action for the robots, is predictable, involves only a small set of actions, and can be achieved through a collaborative search. A theoretical analysis has confirmed that this policy is indeed optimal. In a domain with narrow visibility, a sample set of size 10,000 robots typically achieves this policy in around 5 hours. To further the scope of possible scenarios, an extension has been made to multiple robots in a wide-open space with variable levels of capability. In this expanded context, robots with high vision and low capacity outperform those with low vision and high capacity when they are equally numerous. In this scenario, an optimal policy exists where robots with high vision and low capacity take charge.

A group of objects can be represented in a multidimensional tabular format, where each slot corresponds to a specific combination of characteristics. When each characteristic group has been represented in a similar format, we can combine these representations into a single, unified format, specifically a wreath product, to reflect how the entire group can be broken down based on the defined characteristics. In this paper, we outline a step-by-step approach to determining the structure of the wreath product representation of a given body of objects, which is comprised of various elements that are linked to specific groups of characteristics.

A novel type of optical interferometer has been proposed and analyzed, with the aim of enhancing the performance of gravitational wave detectors at low frequencies. This instrument, the sloshing-Sagncl, employs a gas-filled resonating cavity to improve signal amplification beyond the traditional Sagnac effect. Utilizing the principles of optomechanics, the instrument can be operated in two distinct configurations to optimize performance for detecting gravitational waves and cosmic noise. Theoretical models indicate that this design could offer sensitivity to gravitational waves with frequencies below 10 Hz and meet the requirements for a third-generation ground-based detector. Such a detector would be capable of detecting events with masses as low as 10^-5 M and could even observe the merger of neutron star neutron star binaries within the local universe.

In large-scale MIMO systems with many users, determining the number of active users is crucial to avoid collisions and ensure efficient spectrum usage. A previous study by the authors defined areas where the signal from each user is not interfered with by other users, which takes the form of non-overlapping regions around their locations. The paper aims to calculate the exact size of these non-interfered areas, which are shaped like circles, by employing the distribution of user positions as random and following a Poisson point process model. The authors derive precise formulas for the average areas of these regions, considering both scenarios with and without channel state information. The formulas reveal that the area growth rate is directly proportional to the square of the number of users, which allows the authors to determine the optimal number of users that maximizes the total area. The research also derives the average number of active users, which is found to be cubic in the number of users when CSI is present, but linear when it is not.

Neural text generation models have revolutionized the field of NLP, particularly in language creation tasks, and have been widely used in recent years. Despite the impressive performance of these models, especially in large-scale formats like transformers, there's a growing concern about their size, which can be a significant limitation when applied to tasks like language modeling. To address this issue, our approach introduces a new technique called Residual Learning of Neural Text Creation with an n-gram Language Model, which leverages the efficiency of traditional n-gram models to fill in the gaps of large neural models. Our n-gram based residual learning module learns the short patterns of a language that the large model tends to miss, resulting in a hybrid model that surpasses both the n-gram and neural models in quality. Our code is available on GitHub, and the pre-trained models used in our experiments can be found on Hugging Face.

This study presents an Informed Optical Character Recognition system for tabulating and releasing election ballot totals, which accurately extracts vote counts from printed PDF ballots and their corresponding scanned images. A key advantage of this iOCR system is that it can learn and apply context from the PDF format, eliminating the need for predefined layout information typical in traditional iOCR applications. Our research findings indicate that this iOCR system can effectively tabulate ballot totals for both tested PDF ballot samples in just a few seconds, with error rates significantly lower than 0.01%.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate how various patterns of atmospheric circulation occur around a rotating, warming sphere that resembles Earth. In a lack of detailed computer models, basic conditions such as temperature gradients and the rate of planet spin are examined to determine an underlying pattern of atmospheric circulation that is similar to that found on Earth. A rapid transition is observed when cooler lower layers of the atmosphere become significantly warmer, resulting in a full, global circulation pattern within a few days of model time. A similar pattern is seen when a temperature difference is created between the top and bottom layers of the atmosphere. A situation is also explored where a warm spot is introduced on the model sphere to see if a westward-moving storm pattern develops, similar to one found on Earth. A three-dimensional model with multiple atmospheric layers is used to further investigate the formation of such patterns, with a hot spot of varying sizes and temperatures on the model sphere. A circle of wind flowing around a hot spot is observed when it is small, but a more complex, swirling pattern of wind is seen when the spot is significantly larger and cooler at its edges than at its center. A similar pattern is seen when a temperature difference is created between the top and bottom layers of the atmosphere. A scenario is also explored where a north-south temperature difference is introduced on the model sphere to see if a pattern of westward-moving storms in the middle atmosphere develops, similar to one found on Earth. This study formulates a new expression representing the reciprocal gamma function in terms of a specific integral that incorporates a regularization technique. This expression is derived by linking the reciprocal gamma function to a complex pole through the Bernoulli numbers, and then applying the residue theory. As a result, we obtain an equation that relates the reciprocal gamma function to a circle of convergence, allowing us to extract the real part of the equation and define the desired integral expression.

A quantum fluid's dynamics can be complex, especially when it comes to interacting Bose gases in optical lattans or ultracold gases. To simplify the study of these dynamics, a new hydrodynamic theory has been developed, taking into account both quantum and thermal fluctuations. At the same time, this method ignores the microscopic details of short-wave length density variations. As a result, the theory's short-wave length legitimacy hinges on its consistency with established many-body approaches, such as Bogoliubov free energies. To validate the new method, a developer has derived the linearized hydrodynamic equations, closing the theory by omitting higher-order quantum and thermal correlation contributions. The creator then confirmed the method's accuracy by verifying its quantum and thermal fluctuation descriptions, as well as its consistency with the mentioned free energy approaches. The new hydrodynamic theory should be beneficial for analyzing short-wave length fluctuations in nearly uniform, three-dimensional interacting Bose gases.

The rising trend of knowledge graphs in representing complex information has created a growing need for efficient learning methods that can be applied against these graphs. This demand has given birth to a variety of knowledge acquisition tasks, including relation extraction, classification, and inference. To address these tasks, a new type of machine learning model has emerged, one that learns in a teacher-student framework mimicking traditional educational settings. In this educational framework, an experienced knowledge-bearing model, referred to as the educator or teacher, trains a less experienced model, known as the pupil or student. The pupil's task is to learn from the educator's actions and decisions on a set of graph data. Given the growing size of knowledge graphs and the increasing need for efficient learning strategies, a variety of educator-pupil models have been developed, each with its unique characteristics and learning objectives. This survey provides an in-depth examination of these models, exploring their various learning objectives, frameworks, and optimization algorithms used to train them. It also delves into the multiple evaluation metrics employed to assess the performance of these models and discusses potential future research directions, including applications in knowledge graph construction, multi-task learning, and bi-directional learning.

A compact, efficient function representing the objective of a graphical model has been presented, enabling rapid Exact Maximum Probability Estimation and constrained optimization. This brief function, utilizing a variable elimination approach, bypasses the need for explicit probability table construction, a common graphical model computation. Typically, constructing these tables is a time-consuming and space-intensive process. Aoretical results have been proven, demonstrating the function's accuracy and reliability. Additionally, a practical example has been included, illustrating the function's applicability to latticelike graphical models with continuous random variables.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, particularly with respect to a specific embedding of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within a tensor product. A short exact sequence is then established linking the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ to a series of lower rank centralizers. Utilizing this sequence, a Hilbert-Poincar\'e series is derived for the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. Furthermore, it is shown that this series is identical to a series previously defined in relation to a higher rank Lie algebra known as $U(\mathfrak{g}_A)$, with its simple roots represented by the integer $n$.

The paired-permutation test has gained popularity in data-sensitive areas like healthcare for conducting significance tests. A key challenge in implementing this test lies in efficiently examining structured test scenarios where a random permutation might result in violating scarcity conditions. To address this issue, our method known as Precise Paired-Permutation Examination was developed, aiming to carry out the test without violating these conditions and ensuring the tested hypothesis is paired. Our approach achieves this by combining a naive initial test with precise subsequent tests that may involve multiple permutations. We further derived an algorithm to implement precise tests and calculated its time complexity. Our results demonstrate that our precise method outperforms the naive approach in most scenarios.

Our research examined the structure of an anisotropic ellipse representing a system in a multiphase transport model, specifically when it experiences a sudden change due to an external perturbation. We analyzed this change in elliptical shape for p-p, Au-Au, and Cu-Cu collisions, focusing on the second-order Fourier harmonic $v_2$ and third-order harmonic $v_3$ velocities. To account for varying collision energies (7 TeV, 54.4 GeV, 200 GeV) and particle identification methods (transverse momentum, centrality), we utilized a constant transverse momentum cutoff of 0.4 GeV. Based on elastic and inelastic scattering processes, we observed that both $v_2$ and $v_3$ values closely mimic elliptical particle distribution properties. Notably, we found an ideal orientation allowing particle distribution anisotropy to directly align with elliptical shape characteristics. This alignment results in $v_2$ and $v_3$ values mirroring anisotropy levels. Furthermore, we identified a theoretical limit where $v_3$ anisotropy diminishes due to particle distribution symmetry. To calculate $v_3$ in Au-Au and Cu-Cu collisions, we employed an anisotropic shape correlation method, incorporating previously determined $v_2$ values. A random field central to this paper has a Poisson distribution, leading to a linear Gaussian state model. As a result, implementing a particle filter is theoretically possible. However, in practice, this type of model is highly unlikely, making it unsuitable for most applications, including sensor scheduling, which typically involve numerous sensors.

The dynamics of soccer matches can be highly unpredictable, subjecting teams to a wide range of outcomes even in a single game. This uncertainty makes strategic decision-making extremely complex for coaches, who must balance immediate risks and potential future benefits when choosing formations and making tactical adjustments. In an effort to address this challenge, our research proposes an advanced, context-aware framework for coaching decisions in critical match situations. This framework, which incorporates a combination of reinforcement learning and generative models to analyze and respond to evolving match dynamics, was tested on a large dataset of real soccer matches. Our results indicate that our context-aware policy consistently outperforms a more basic, historical policy in terms of winning probability, with a notable improvement observed in high-stakes situations such as leading by a goal or trailing by a goal. Notably, our policy never engages in extremely risky actions like scoring multiple goals in a single match period, demonstrating a natural capacity for risk management.

A cost-effective and efficient approach is presented to enable a single-point Laser Doppler Velocimeter (LDV) system to acquire two-dimensional velocity measurements. This is achieved through the simultaneous use of a stereo Pair Correlation Velocimeter (PCV) and the LDV, with both systems operated at distinct frequencies to allow for independent data collection. A stereo PCV provides three-dimensional velocity information, whereas a single-point LDV delivers instantaneous velocity data. To calculate two-dimensional velocity distributions, a POD-based optimization is employed to position the LDV measurement point optimally. A turbulent flow over a circular cylinder is used as a test case, with both systems used to gather data at different locations. The results show excellent agreement between the LDV and PCV measurements for both the mean and rms values of velocity. The results are also compared to PIV data from a similar study to validate the accuracy of the method.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that combines the Klein--Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

In experiments involving particle collisions, identifying neutral long-lived particles relies on their decays into observable products. This reliance is particularly significant for searches involving missing energy signatures, such as those found in processes involving dark matter or axion-like particles. Despite the challenges, some decay scenarios offer promising opportunities for detection, especially when the particle's lengthened lifetime results in visible decay products outside the immediate collision area. This is the case for certain A-scale particle (ALP) masses, ranging from a few hundred million to a few billion GeV, which could potentially be discovered through decays into visible final states in experiments like Belle II or a future e+e- collider. Such discoveries could pave the way for further investigation using advanced detector technologies, such as a 100 GeV-energy scale that would allow Belle II to identify decays resulting in particles like an electron and a photon, or a 10 GeV-momentum scale that would enable the Belle II or a future e+e- collider to pinpoint decays into a single photon. Moreover, in scenarios where ALPs interact weakly with matter, their decay into pairs of photons could be facilitated, leading to possible detection methods, such as using a magnetic field to deflect neutral particles or employing a detector with a large mass sensitivity, such as a time projection chamber. This study provides a detailed analysis of the fluctuations in word meanings over time, examining how contextual language models and their counterparts, both statically and dynamically trained, perceive these changes. A dataset was created consisting of 20,000 English words with their semantic changes mapped out across three periods: past, present, and future. To evaluate the models' ability to identify contextually varying word meanings, three distinct methodologies were employed. Initially, contextualized models were tested on words exhibiting clear semantic shifts, then on words with steady meanings, and finally on words with little available data. The results showed that models trained on large datasets, such as Wikidata and Wikipedia, performed better than those trained on general text data. Notably, the dynamically trained models outperformed their statically trained counterparts. Contextualized models that performed well on words with notable shifts in meaning did not necessarily excel on words with consistent meanings. Words with little available data presented a challenge for all models. To further investigate these findings, an experiment was conducted where contextualized models were presented with contextually stable words and words with varying meanings. The results revealed that models often failed to distinguish between these two categories of words. This failure is attributed to the models' tendency to pick up on the most frequent semantic associations, leaving them ill-equipped to identify contextually varying word meanings. To address this issue, an idea was proposed to create a new type of word representation that would capture the unique characteristics of words with shifting meanings. To determine if this method can identify such particles, we must establish a minimum mass limit for 10^8 M_solar black holes by considering the stability of the AGN jet and the electron cooling time. Quantum harmonic oscillators have long been a fundamental system of interest for both classical and quantum mechanics. In this study, we examine a driven quantum harmonic oscillator, a variant that has garnered significant attention in the context of applied quantum field theory, particularly in the 1980s and 1990s. This research employs path integral methods to investigate this system, with a focus on a specific driving force that causes the oscillator to transition between two distinct energy levels. This transition results in a non-trivial distribution of the oscillator's energy, leading to a phase transition where the system's quantum behavior is significantly amplified. To analyze this phase transition, we employ Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations, a widely used stochastic method that generates random samples from complex probability distributions. In this case, we simulate the distribution of the oscillator's energy by generating random paths that represent possible quantum states. By applying path integral formalism, we can calculate the energy distribution of the oscillator, along with critical driving strength and temperature values that signify the phase transition. Notably, our results demonstrate excellent agreement with established theoretical predictions, particularly the Gaussian approximation and the critical exponent. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of the phase transition in driven quantum harmonic oscillators, a system that has garnered significant interest in the context of applied quantum field theory, particularly in the 1980s and 1990s. We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare calculus to accommodate an innovative type system that incorporates "expectations." This calculus is designed to verify programs ensuring specific relationships between data. The preconditions and postconditions of a program can be represented as relational pairs, which are treated as abstract data that a program may manipulate. This Hoare calculus differs from traditional calculi as it allows preconditions and postconditions to be complex programs that can be executed, based on a previous verification of their behavior. This adaptation extends previous quantum relational Hoare calculus, enabling the validation of programs that implement bi-partite protocols, such as quantum teleportation, and demonstrates its effectiveness by verifying several protocols.

A pervasive issue in solar physics, bias in data affects magnetogram derivatives like vertical height above the photosphere and magnetic field strength. Since the Sun's vector magnetic field is derived from these values, a bias can also be present. We observe that a bias, specifically a correlation between the error and latitude, exists in the Sun's magnetic field's longitudinal component. However, since the component's measurement approach varies between different instruments, pinpointing the source is challenging. To investigate further, we examine how a non-linear least-squares inversion algorithm, utilised to calculate the vector magnetic field, interacts with the biased derivative data. Initially, we simulate an ideal scenario with negligible noise. In this case, the bias doesn't affect the output, as the inversion algorithm accurately accounts for magnetic field polarity. Next, we introduce an instrumental bias mimicking a 1000-degrees height discrepancy. The algorithm fails to produce accurate results, as it cannot distinguish between magnetic field polarity and inclination. Since the Sun's magnetic field's polarity is well-established, the bias shouldn't affect the output. To further investigate, we create an artificial, biased magnetogram pattern with a varying amplitude. The algorithm correctly compensates for the bias as it prioritises magnetic field polarity. To better understand the bias's nature, we contact the NSO/GONG and HELAS data providers. They confirm that their instrument calibration files show no significant discrepancies in measured photospheric magnetic field longitudes. Since the bias doesn't appear in the calibration

This study investigates the concept of applying Boolean functions to involutions, a type of permutation that returns to its original form after reversal. Our primary focus is on determining the conditions under which an n-dimensional involution permutation meets the criteria of being a (weak) Boolean function. We begin by analyzing 2-dimensional involutions and derive a comprehensive set of rules that classify Boolean functions within this specific dimension. Additionally, we identify a polynomial sequence that represents Boolean functions among involutions within the 2-dimensional space. Subsequent sections explore more complex n-dimensional involutions, identifying a key pattern that satisfies the Boolean function requirement. A construction method is also established to generate Boolean functions among n-dimensional involutions, allowing even even n values by introducing a new type of permutation called the "twisted (n+2)-regular 90-degree rotation" that incorporates an (n+2)-dimensional space.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in a 4-dimensional semi-Riemannian space with a metric of the form (-++++), satisfy certain conditions if they meet specific geometric criteria. A curve that is a local extremum in terms of a specific energy functional will adhere to a particular straight line pattern if its associated curve, defined by a certain distance measurement, also meets the same geometric classification.

A tiny change in loss function wording has a significant impact on a deep learning model's performance in a medical diagnosis task, according to our findings. Our research reveals that even the slightest change in phrasing can lead to a model predicting a condition that is 10 times more likely. In such a binary classification task where words change slightly, our results show that the way loss is calculated and optimized has a crucial impact on model predictions. Our key discovery indicates that models are biased towards giving priority to the first word of a classification category, resulting in an increased risk of misdiagnosing conditions with more complex names. With three common medical conditions, our experiments demonstrate that loss function adjustment can significantly improve model accuracy from 70% to almost 100% without degrading its ability to learn from data.

Our proposed atlas, ATOMIC, is an extensive compilation of logical knowledge in the form of 'if-then' statements, intentionally created to facilitate human imitation tasks and the development of reasoning algorithms. Unlike other knowledge bases that categorize information topically or hierarchically, ATOMIC organizes knowledge in conditional relationships, mirroring how it is naturally structured and enabling the evaluation of reasoning algorithms along these lines. To build ATOMIC, we gathered a large dataset of 'if-then' statements from a popular video sharing platform, consisting of approximately 340,000 unique instances and 240,000 unique premises. This atlas has several advantages, as demonstrated by the success of our proposed evaluation metrics in assessing the performance of reasoning algorithms and the achievement of state-of-the-art results in various reasoning tasks.

This study proposes an advanced video forecasting method that predicts future views of complex objects from simple overhead views of a 2D environment containing multiple objects. The proposed approach uses a two-part representation of the environment, consisting of bird's eye view (BEV) and top-down view (TDV) maps, to forecast a specific view of an object with an rotating or extending body. Initially, a simple model forecasts the BEV structure of the environment, then a more complex model forecasts the TDV representation of the view in question. The key view can be obtained from the TDV representation through perspective projection. The research was conducted using a variety of grid and polygon-based environments with randomly positioned objects and achieved the best results compared to a baseline approach, with the simple BEV model contributing significantly to performance.

A graph is considered fully measurable or metrically embeddable when the set of distances between its distinct points is sufficient to determine the graph's structure.  The shortest path distance between points A and B in a graph G is defined as the minimum length of a path connecting A and B.  A subset S of vertices is considered a measuring set if it can determine the distances between all pairs of vertices based on their distances to members of S.  The minimum size of a measuring set is referred to as the metric dimension of the graph.  Research on the metric dimension of various graph types has led to establishing formulas and bounds.  However, determining the exact metric dimension of most graphs is not a straightforward task as it involves calculating the smallest number of points whose distances can define the graph's structure.  In a 2016 study, it was found that certain graph types, including trees, have a metric dimension of either 1 or 2, depending on their structure.  On the other hand, a simple line graph with five vertices arranged in a square shape with an additional vertex connected to all others has a metric dimension of 3.  It is also noted that certain graph types, such as circles and ladders, have specific metric dimension characteristics based on their size.  Beyond these specific instances, additional research is needed to explore the metric dimension of various graph types. Early detection of heart conditions such as murmurs is critical, and point-cutting techniques like stetoscopy have been used to aid doctors in listening for these issues. However, their effectiveness can be compromised when background noise interferes with the sound, and a better method is needed to overcome this limitation. In this research, we propose a new technique called "Local Contrast Enhancement Network" (LCEN) to help doctors identify heart murmurs despite background noise and other challenges. To validate our approach, we conducted a series of experiments using a combination of synthetic and real-world data, and the results showed that our method outperformed other noise-reduction techniques and met the requirements for real-world applications.

To better understand the physical conditions and behavior of molecular gas within galaxies, a new study examines how excitation temperatures are determined for $^{3}$P$_{1}$ $\rightarrow$ $^{3}$P$_{2}$ transitions in $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO. A key finding is that $^{12}$CO(1-0) and $^{12}$CO(2-1) are typically not in LTE with the gas temperature, even in the most massive galaxies. This non-equilibrium condition has implications for how dust temperatures are calculated from CO data. Additionally, it's found that $^{12}$CO(1-0) and CII$\lambda$157.7.0 are generally in LTE with each other. This mutual equilibrium allows for a more precise method of determining CO excitation temperatures. A new formula is derived that calculates excitation temperatures without requiring assumptions about CO brightness or sensitivity to line fluxes. This new formula is particularly useful for $^{13}$CO(1-0) and can help determine $^{12}$CO(1-1) excitation temperatures when $^{12}$CO(2-1) is not available. This research is significant as it provides a more accurate way of calculating CO excitation temperatures, which is crucial for calculating molecular gas masses. This improved method also enables the calculation of $^{12}$CO(4-3) and $^{13}$CO(2-1) exc

In 2010, a key paper titled "The ASEP velocity process" was published by P. Nejjar, further advancing the ASEP's velocity process analysis initially explored by T. Seiler in 2005. This paper delves into the ASEP's velocity process at an arbitrary positive angle less than 2*pi, within the context of a lattice that is infinite in two dimensions. The author's primary goal is to identify the probability measure governing this process, which aligns with previous findings by T. Seiler for specific angles including 45 degrees. The paper's methodology involves analyzing the ASEP's transition probabilities, which mirror those of an ASEP that is known to be driven by a product measure. The product measure in question resembles the Bethe-Boltzmann equilibrium measure, which is used to define the desired probability distribution. The paper's key contribution lies in establishing an integral representation of the ASEP's velocity process's probability density function, which is crucial for future applications.

The rapid spread of SARS-CoV-2 across the globe has created an unprecedented crisis, necessitating a multidisciplinary approach that incorporates epidemiological models to predict and manage the pandemic effectively. In the early stages of outbreaks, mathematical models play a critical role in understanding disease dynamics, evaluating control strategies, and providing critical data for policy-makers. We examine various models used to analyze SARS-CoV-2, including basic reproductive number models, network models, serological models and models that account for vaccine distribution, highlighting their strengths and limitations. We also discuss the importance of incorporating real-time data into models to ensure their accuracy and applicability. Furthermore, we outline the potential role of mathematical models in post-pandemic research, emphasizing the need to predict and mitigate the risk of future outbreaks.

A significant positive correlation exists between the stellar mass (M*) of galaxies and their star formation rates (SFR) on average. However, this trend reverses when considering the formation of bulges within massive galaxies, which may contribute to a decline in SFR at high M* levels. To investigate this transition from a linear to an inverted pattern, we conducted an analysis that accounts for the presence of bulges in galaxies. Our results show that when considering bulge and total stellar masses separately, the SFR is consistently more active around low to intermediate mass ranges but becomes more dormant at high mass levels. This inverted pattern is more pronounced when focusing on bulge stellar masses rather than total stellar masses. This finding suggests that the growth of bulges might be the primary factor driving the shift from a positive to a negative SFR-M* correlation. Additionally, we observed that galaxies with higher bulge-to-total stellar mass ratios exhibit lower SFRs, even after adjusting for factors such as redshift, metallicity, and the presence of an active galactic nucleus. This implies that the presence and growth of bulges are key factors influencing SFR and M* relationships.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news headlines to predict stock market movements. Our
method employs multi-task learning with a sentiment prediction task and a
language identification task to process data in multiple languages. We used a
small sentiment dataset but a large language ID dataset, demonstrating that
the paper's approach can effectively utilize a vast amount of language ID info
to learn sentiment prediction. Our network produced promising results on a
set of languages, including English, outperforming other methods, and our
experiments showed a positive correlation between positive headlines and
stock gains in multiple languages.

If a planet with a low mass and a short period falls into a massive orbit around a distant star, it may eventually cross the star's convective zone, risking its disintegration. In such a scenario, some models suggest that the planetary material could potentially infiltrate the star, potentially even merging with its core. If this theory holds true, it could provide an explanation for the observed rapid spin of certain stars, such as KIC 9267654, which features a short axis rotation period of about 1.5 hours. In this specific case, a low-mass planet with an unusually high angular momentum might have entered the star, possibly even breaking apart within the convective zone, transferring its spin to the star in the process. To verify this hypothesis, astronomers conducted a detailed analysis of multiple stars, including KIC 9267654, which showed that only a small fraction of stars with short rotation periods exceeding 10 hours exhibit similar characteristics of high angular momentum. What they found was that these stars typically have low surface temperatures, are massive, and have short periods of about 5 days or less. Conversely, stars with higher angular momentum more frequently exhibit cooler surface temperatures, are more massive, and have more substantial radii. What they also discovered was that planets with low masses and short orbital periods around massive stars often inherit high angular momentum, which they can then transfer to the star if they enter its convective zone. False news rapidly spreads across social media platforms due to its timely publication, making quick detection crucial. Although automated systems can effectively identify false news by analyzing real-time data, they may also create false information through generative models like chatbots and artificial intelligence. This newly emerging false news can potentially evade traditional false news detection methods that rely on pre-trained models and trained data. To address this issue, an approach has been proposed that utilizes a meta-learning, sparse, distributed, memory-based neural process network capable of learning from a minimal amount of pre-existing information and rapidly adapting to new information with only a few data points. This approach demonstrates a test accuracy of 92.5% on a small dataset and 85.5% on a larger dataset consisting of 10,000 samples, collected from Twitter and verified by fact-checking organizations.

Recently, a novel type of Golay complementary sets called the Golay complementary arrays has been introduced and demonstrated to facilitate simultaneous omnidirectional omnigain and omnidirectional gain measurements in the frequency domain for multiple, concurrent users in wireless communication systems. To accomplish omnidirectional omnidirectional gain, pairs of orthogonal signals are required, whereas this is already satisfied by pairs of complementary signals. On the other hand, achieving omnidirectional gain in the frequency domain for each of the possible combinations of four signals proves more complicated and could be achieved through the creation of a pair of 4x4 Golay complementary matrices or, alternatively, a pair of 2D Golay complementary arrays with a size of 4x4.

A novel method for creating realistic cerebral lesion maps has been developed, utilizing a progressive adversarial variational autoencoder. This encoder-decoder model is trained on a large dataset of brain scans with varying lesion sizes to produce high-definition lesion masks. To ensure the generated masks resemble actual cerebral lesions, a classification module is employed, incorporating a convolutional neural network to classify lesions into five categories. This classification step enables the model to learn meaningful representations of lesion characteristics. In contrast to existing methods, this approach generates both the lesion mask and the underlying brain structure without the need for a pre-defined format or external segmentation steps. This cerebral lesion generation model outperforms current techniques, demonstrating excellent performance on both lesion synthesis and segmentation tasks.

A new unified framework has been developed to tackle both supervised and semi-supervised feature extraction tasks. The method, dubbed CFX, employs a comparative learning approach that utilizes relative comparisons between data points. This comparison is represented as a binary vector, which the authors show can be used to create a new drift-aware feature learning algorithm. The algorithm's initial phase generates a set of comparison patterns unique to each data point, which are then used to construct a new set of linear projections that enhance classification performance. The authors' experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of CFX in both supervised and semi-supervised scenarios, outperforming existing methods in multiple datasets.

Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have yielded impressive performance, particularly in tasks like question answering and generative writing. To further enhance the capabilities of LLMs in specific domains, there's a growing interest in tailored models that focus on particular skills or knowledge areas. This paper proposes an innovative framework called Ability, which efficiently incorporates structured information into LMs. This framework is particularly suitable for creating models with diverse abilities, such as understanding mathematical proofs, recognizing artistic styles, and grasping medical diagnoses. To demonstrate the effectiveness of Ability, the authors developed a suite of models that excel in various tasks, including identifying musical genres and analyzing sports data. These models delivered superior performance compared to generic LLMs, often by a significant margin of up to 60%. Furthermore, Ability's capabilities can be easily updated to accommodate new knowledge areas without overhauling the underlying model.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in a vacuum refractive index. This, in turn, creates a shadow with an asymmetric radius around a black hole's event horizon. We investigate how this effect impacts the first-order principles of thermodynamics, including energy conservation, the Clausius inequality, and the Noether theorem, when applied to a non-linear electrovascular black hole. Additionally, we examine how this non-linear interaction affects the radii of both the event horizon and the shadow, as well as the mass and temperature of the black hole, in accordance with horizon dynamics. A cascade of nonlinear interactions will lead to a cascade of higher-order curvature terms on the event horizon, resulting in a distended shadow with an axis of symmetry around the central source. We model this distribution using a generalized analytic function, specifically a Mittag-Leffler function, and derive a thermodynamic description by calculating the energy density. The analysis reveals that the thermal energy of the shadow complements the energy of the black hole, allowing us to define a new, combined energy metric. We also derive a universal relation between the non-linear electric field, the radius of the shadow, and the energy metric of the shadow, in addition to another relation involving the mass and temperature of the black hole.

Reconstructing an accurate picture of a quantum system's state is crucial, especially when it comes to understanding how its entanglement evolves over time. For a system like an optical one, consisting of two continuous variables, a method called "state reconstruction" is essential. This paper proposes novel approaches to discern even the slightest changes in how closely entangled two light particles are, as well as how synchronized their properties are. These methods apply to both macroscopic and microscopic systems, emphasizing their importance in understanding quantum systems' behavior.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions are determined as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*2}_0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fractions are estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6)×10^-4 and (3.5±1.4±0.3±0.3±0.6)×10^-4 respectively, with the latter decay mode including a 1.4±0.6×10^-4 background contribution from $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ decay modes that have been subtracted.

A polynomial construction is used to build the lattice of submodules of a given module $M$, excluding free modules, based on its character table and the lattices of its submodules corresponding to its irreducible constituents.

We investigate how certain operators affect Biharmonic hypersurfaces within the Euclidean space, particularly when these surfaces are subjected to repeated applications of these effects at a specific point.

A subset of integers is identifiable under a rational number p/q if for any two distinct subsets of the integers, having the same intersection as a set of integers that is defined by the predicate defined by p/q, will have a difference that is visible to sets defined by intervals of length (p/q). In other words, if the predicate defined by p/q identifies any two distinct subsets of the integers, then it is a reliable method for identifying them. The main aim of this paper is to investigate the largest size that can be achieved by sets that are identifiable under a given rational number p/q.

A persistent auditory phenomenon observed during adhesive tape unpeeling has been analyzed both physically and mathematically. Contrary to initial impressions of random noise, our measurements reveal a hidden periodic pattern in the sounds emitted as the tape unrolls. To better understand this pattern, we employed Fourier analysis and identified a direct correlation between the frequency of the sounds and the unrolling speed. Based on these findings, a theoretical model was developed to explain the emergence of these periodic sounds, centered around the creation of air pockets between the tape's layers. This model confirms that the pattern's frequency is directly tied to the unrolling speed. In situations where the unrolling speed remains constant, the pattern will transition from a single-tone sound to a harmonic series, resulting in a more complex pattern. In such cases, additional peaks will appear in the Fourier spectrum. This research provides a comprehensive explanation of the underlying physics driving the periodic sounds produced during adhesive tape unpeeling, aligning with previous studies on similar phenomena in physical systems.

In 1930, K. Menger developed an abstract concept of space that incorporates the idea of measuring angles between curves, and he defined an n-dimensional metric phase space. We have taken Menger's definition and adapted it to work with the concept of n-dimensional metric geometric spaces. We have also used this version to define a space that is of n-dimensional metric geometric type, and we have established that these types of spaces coincide when the underlying dimension matches.

A new technique called TPC is proposed, consisting of randomizing non-sensitive parts of point cloud structures to enhance privacy. This method is specifically designed to utilize a newly introduced privacy property called the 'Transformation Invariance' principle. It is demonstrated that typical randomization techniques based on Euclidean distance satisfy this invariance property; however, this specific property is not sufficient for creating a method that could be used to determine an optimal transformation. A theoretical model is developed to determine an optimal Gaussian distribution with maximum variance when the structure is projected onto a specific line. Additionally, it is possible to apply a 3D Gaussian transformation to a structure by applying it to each point of the structure. It is shown that a Gaussian distribution with a standard deviation of 0.1 meets the requirements of privacy; a theoretical bound of 10.6 is derived for the number of points in a structure to maintain privacy. The TPC method is highly efficient as it only requires applying a Gaussian distribution to each point of the structure. It is shown that the TPC method satisfies the invariance principle; a specific analysis is conducted to determine the number of points required to determine the transformation. It is possible to use existing privacy verification methods such as VPE and RNE; however, they may not be the most efficient options. To accurately evaluate programs based on their output, we have developed a new framework that utilizes geometric concepts, particularly the Levenshtein distance in metric spaces. At the heart of this framework lies the idea of comparing programs by analyzing the similarity between their outputs, which can take various forms such as strings, trees, or even more complex structures like graphs. This approach allows us to measure the quality of programs based on how closely their outputs match the desired outcome, which is represented as a distance value. In a simple string output scenario, this distance translates to an error bound, ensuring that programs with a distance of 1 or less from the optimal one will produce identical outputs. To further analyze program performance, we introduce an idea of "epsilon-close" programs, which are those with output distances less than or equal to some predefined value epsilon. By defining a set of programs that are epsilon-close to the best program, we can derive an upper bound on their number, which is crucial for evaluating the quality of the best program. In more complex output structures, such as tree outputs, we observe that the Levenshtehe distance is not effective but can be replaced by more suitable measures like the edit distance for structured data. In such cases, we find that an error bound of 1 ensures identical output for programs with a distance of 1. We provide a detailed explanation for determining the weights of the second Chern class in the context of the mod p cohomology of GL(2) through Kummer theory. This approach bypasses the involvement of local fields and their properties.

Advanced composite materials with self-sensing capabilities are being researched for their potential to detect damage through changes in electrical conductivity following material failure. A key challenge in utilizing this technology lies in accurately identifying damage locations. A new approach utilizing Genetic Algorithms and Inverse Problems aims to pinpoint precise damage shapes within composite materials. In a single-layer NDE composite lamina with a circular hole under uniform tensile stress, a small elliptical notch causes a distinct conductivity pattern on the surface, which can be effectively mapped by EIT. Scanning the material creates a 2D image of conductivity variations, which indicate contact points between broken carbon fibers within the damaged area. Further analysis reveals that the pattern correlates with the notch's geometric characteristics. Using a PZT sensor as the driving source provides high-frequency information at the notch's center, resulting in the most detailed image. Utilizing this information, an GA-based inverse method accurately identifies the notch's shape. Similar results are obtained with a curved notch and multiple notches of varying shapes. In all cases, the method accurately reconstructs the notch's geometry from the EIT images. The most complex scenario involves three interconnected notches of different sizes and shapes, which the GA-based approach successfully maps with high precision. The most significant area of distortion corresponds to the largest notch, the second-most significant area corresponds to the medium-sized notch, and the smallest area corresponds to the smallest notch. The method's accuracy is confirmed by comparing the reconstructed shapes to the actual notches. The

This work delves into the metrics of a Euclidean n-dimensional space when it is represented as a tensor. A key point is that these geometric measures - both short and long distances, as well as angles - can be defined in terms of the inner product within the vector space of linear transformations that represents this space. A normal transformation matrix fits into a special category of linear transformations that are defined by an inner product, making its corresponding geometric measures directly equivalent to specific values. For instance, in a 3-dimensional space, a short radius is represented by a measure of pi/3, a long radius is represented as 2*pi/3, a right angle is represented as pi/2, and a straight angle is represented as pi. These predefined measures allow for the mapping of geometric characteristics to specific topological spaces, making possible the construction of manifolds with complex geometric patterns by combining individual features.

A right-angled Artin group is a kind of group that has received significant mathematical interest, particularly in areas of geometry, topology, and group theory. A key characteristic of a right-angled Artin group is that it can be defined by a set of generators and a set of relations, where these relations are essentially free from redundancy. A fundamental aspect of understanding this type of group is determining the length of the shortest word that represents a given element within the group. This specific element in question is a product of generators in various combinations, which are linked by an edge in a certain graph associated with the group. This graph is crucial in analyzing the structure of the group. A significant subset of this graph, consisting of disconnected components, can be used to define a smaller group, known as a quotient group, which inherits various properties from the original group. A key property of this quotient group is that its length can be directly determined based on the lengths of the original group, in addition to the distance between generators in the graph. A key result in this study is that the longest element in the quotient group corresponds to a product of generators that is separated by a path of a specific length in the graph. A key aspect of this research is defining the length of a path in the graph, which can be quite complex in certain scenarios. A notable type of path, known as an induced path, can be created by linking an edge between two vertices if there exists a third vertex that is connected to both

A novel algorithm is presented that expedites the performance of matrix inversion by merely a factor of 2^(d-1) when d levels of recursion are used, despite the fact that matrix dimensions grow with 2^d. This algorithm's d=4 implementation delivers impressive performance on GPU architectures, specifically 1.4 million iterations per second on an NVIDIA A100 device, whereas classic O(n^3) algorithms like LU decomposition or CUDA-based implementations fall short, only matching the new approach for d=1.

Contextual linear Gibbs is a context-aware model with locally developed actions, where both context and action are vector-based. This research demonstrates how a contextual linear Gibbs model with locally developed actions can be learned in a distributed environment without sharing the context. This is achieved through a combination of a gradient-based learning algorithm and a contextual linear model with locally developed actions that uses a third representation of the context. This third representation is a low-dimensional space where the context is embedded. This paper's initial contribution is a gradient-based learning algorithm that updates the linear weights and the distribution over the observable actions in the low-dimensional context representation space. The second contribution is a bound derived on the regret experienced by an agent that uses this algorithm. In a typical situation, the agent's regret is small.

A weak instability in a protoplanetary disk's outer region may lead to dust growth, which in turn could potentially create a stronger instability. To examine the effects of this stronger instability, we've expanded our previous stability model to include both radial and vertical shear, as well as the sediments' settling behavior. When considering both dust species with varying sizes, we find that an instability can arise in the outer region following a pattern of decreasing altitude. This type of instability may facilitate the development of non-linear density patterns, which could influence the sedimentation process and growth rate of particles. As a result, a density bump may form near the inner edge of the $10\mu$m radius band, potentially leading to the sediment's rapid growth and creation of a gap. With a maximum sediment radius of $1$mm, a gap can form near the $10$AU radius band, which may then expand to $30$AU when the sediment growth reaches $1$cm in size. However, this may not occur if the sediment growth results in a low-to-medium optical depth, leading to the disappearance of the instability and the sediment growth slowing down.

This study investigates the harmonic and the Yamabe harmonic operator functionality in the context of a Ricci diminished manifold that possesses a constant scalar curvature. The obtained results demonstrate the following: the Liouville equations' solutions are universally achieved for both the harmonic and the Yamabe harmonic operator functionality. Additionally, an equivalence is established between the Liouville equation's solutions and the zero function property of the harmonic and the Yamabe harmonic operator functionality. The study's findings also utilize the obtained results to examine a stability issue in the context of a Ricci diminished manifold that possesses a constant scalar curvature.

Recent advancements in vision transformers have led to success in various computer vision tasks. As a result, our team developed a new transformer-based architecture called the Dynamic Entrance with Global Mean Pooling, aiming to enhance video recognition performance. Our initial experiments with Kinetics-406 and TAMI datasets yielded promising results. Our model achieved top-1 accuracy of 76.0% on a subset of the Kinetics-406 dataset and outperformed the current state-of-the-art score of 74.6% on the TAMI dataset. Our findings suggest that our approach excels in local recognition tasks.

In the context of a widely studied learning algorithm, a team of researchers has explored an innovative, random gradient-based learning process for a simple regression task. They have proposed a new, efficient learning-from-logs protocol to accurately calculate variance and a gradient descent algorithm with varying step sizes to determine optimal step size bounds. A new algorithm, 'Stroll' has been introduced, which incorporates a random walk component to adjust the learning rate and a gradient descent phase to update the model. In a scenario with multiple learners, Stroll has been shown to learn a model with high accuracy and low risk of exploitation, demonstrating significant improvements over existing methods. In a single learner scenario with a large range of possible values, significant performance gains have been observed, with Stroll achieving the best results for both small and large datasets.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a novel regularization technique that ensures consistency between annotated label pixels and the network's predicted segments. Unlike existing methods that rely on sophisticated generative models, this technique leverages the existing learned representation. By incorporating this regularizer into the semi-supervised training process, our approach significantly improves medical image segmentation performance. Our technique's simplicity and effectiveness are demonstrated through a series of experiments on publicly available datasets, including the publicly available MICCAI challenges' datasets: HPA and HBU. Our results show that our method outperforms existing semi-supervised techniques, with our best model achieving remarkable segmentation accuracy of 92.8% on the HPA dataset and 94.4% on the HBU dataset.

In quantum optics, both partial and full entanglement have been widely studied for their distinct properties. Specifically, the phenomena of steering, which occurs when the state of one particle is manipulated by measuring another, has been examined in relation to entanglement. A recent study claiming genuine single-particle entanglement leads to new effects not seen in fully entangled states has been disputed. Our research reveals that both genuine single-particle entanglement and full entanglement are indistinguishable from a non-local entangled state known as a Schr\"odinger cat, thereby eliminating the possibility of single-particle entanglement producing unique optical effects.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems has significantly enhanced the functionality of Internet of Vehicles (IoVs). However, the existing infrastructure and the need for real-time processing have created security challenges and vulnerabilities. As IoVs systems are highly complex and sophisticated, typical safety threats have evolved into more sophisticated risks such as hacking into vehicle navigation systems and manipulating critical control systems. Furthermore, the typical safety threats of IoVs have transformed into risks of data privacy and security as various vehicles generate vast amounts of data that require AI processing. As a result, ensuring the privacy and security of this data has become a pressing concern. Blockchain technology, renowned for its robust security properties, has been explored for possible applications in IoVs systems, including data sharing, intelligent driving, and AI decision-making. A new architecture that combines Blockchain and AI has shown promising results in various IoVs scenarios, demonstrating significant improvements in security and privacy. Notably, research has also been conducted on the creation of accurate AI models through a method called Federated Learning, which has been applied to various IoVs scenarios including intelligent driving, traffic prediction, and vehicle control. This research has yielded promising outcomes in data privacy and security. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring multiple scenarios, including intelligent driving, vehicle control, data sharing, and AI model privacy. This comprehensive survey provides a thorough analysis of the current state of Blockchain and FL technologies, examining their potential applications, challenges, and possible

A practical and efficient LSTM network is proposed for video identification, with a reduced computational footprint and low power consumption. A combination of RRAM and FPGAs is used for implementing the design, with a focus on memory-efficient video feature extraction and a new LSTM architecture. The new LSTM structure omits multiplication operations within memory, utilizing only weight storage in RRAM and weights closer to the data in a cascade manner. This results in better performance and lower costs compared to traditional LSTMs, with a 47.5% area reduction and a 3.9x decrease in memory access latency. The design achieves high accuracy and outperforms current video identification methods, with an accuracy of 97.1% on a large-scale dataset and a low latency of 120ms. This results in a significant boost in throughput of 13.5x and a reduction in computational complexity by 77%.

In a recent paper, a team of authors established that iterates of composite functions, with a specific structure, can be effectively computed at a prime p by transforming the functions modulo p in a more manageable way. This initial research serves as a foundation for our current work, where we have significantly expanded the underlying identity and its implications. A key contribution is a straightforward, step-by-step guide for determining the degree of the iterated composite function, addressing a notable gap in their proof. Additionally, we have derived a crucial formula for computing the iterates of the transformed functions, eliminating the need for polynomial multiplication. A notable application of our findings lies in resolving a long-standing problem concerning the computability of iterates of functions in algebraic complexity theory, specifically involving functions defined as compositions of basic polynomial maps. This resolution enables us to demonstrate that iterates of such functions can be efficiently computed at any prime p, aligning with our initial identity's implications.
